query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A data‐driven ML model that integrates ab initio descriptors for defect and oxygen-induced scattering will predict the temperature‐dependent conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr (with ~1 wt% oxygen contamination) within experimental uncertainty, outperforming traditional perfect‐crystal analytical methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy as produced experimentally, containing intrinsic structural defects and approximately 1 wt% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Develop and train an ML model that incorporates both first-principles derived descriptors and explicit defect/impurity scattering parameters (including oxygen content) to simulate conductivity across temperature.
generation.conditions: The model is applied over two temperature regimes: a low-temperature regime (0–200 K) where defect scattering dominates and a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K) where phonon scattering is significant, with oxygen levels maintained near 1 wt%.
generation.structural_mediator: Defect-induced microstructural disorder, notably due to oxygen contamination, which alters electron scattering behavior in the lattice.
generation.mechanism: By combining ab initio calculations with empirical data on defect scattering, the ML model explicitly captures how impurities and lattice imperfections modify both electron-phonon and impurity scattering contributions, yielding temperature- and sample-specific conductivity predictions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predicted conductivities will closely match experimental measurements (within ±5% at 300 K) and accurately follow the known trends in both low- and high-temperature regimes, thereby reducing the systematic error observed in defect-free models.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical predictions based on perfect, defect-free crystals typically show deviations greater than ±20% from measured values in real specimens.
generation.boundary: The predictive accuracy is expected to hold for bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys with oxygen contamination near 1 wt% and for temperatures ranging from 0 to 1200 K. Extrapolations beyond these impurity levels or temperature limits may require additional calibration.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement and the relative contributions of various scattering mechanisms remain uncertain due to complexities in defect distribution and microstructural heterogeneity, which could affect the ML model’s generalizability.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the ML model to predict the room-temperature (300 K) conductivity for a held-out specimen of bulk HfNbTaTiZr with ~1 wt% oxygen. Then, conduct a series of experiments to measure the electrical conductivity at 300 K, as well as across the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured room-temperature conductivity deviates by more than ±20% from the model’s prediction (or if the temperature-dependent trends do not align with predictions), then the hypothesis that the ML model can accurately account for defect-induced scattering is falsified.

Through this paper, we show that it is possible to use machine learning (ML) in this arena for phase prediction to develop novel HEAs. This was necessary to avoid the discrepancy inherent with comparing HEAs obtained from different synthesis routes as it causes spurious effects while treating an imbalanced data—an erroneous practice we observed in the reported literature. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a promising class of materials with exceptional structural and functional properties. However, their design and optimization pose challenges due to the large composition-phase space coupled with the complex and diverse nature of the phase formation dynamics. In this study, a data-driven approach that utilizes machine learning (ML) techniques to predict HEA phases and their composition-dependent phases is proposed. By employing a comprehensive dataset comprising 5692 experimental records encompassing 50 elements and 11 phase categories, we compare the performance of various ML models. Our analysis identifies the most influential features for accurate phase prediction. Furthermore, the class imbalance is addressed by employing data augmentation methods, raising the number of records to 1500 in each category, and ensuring a balanced representation of phase categories. The results show that XGBoost and Random Forest consistently outperform the other models, achieving 86% accuracy in predicting all phases. In recent years, many works have introduced computational methods to identify and characterize alloys with tailored properties, such as the solid solution strengthening, hardness, ductility index, and thermodynamic stability. Moreover, some of these methods have been employed in the context of the optimization of several target properties,, with the relevant material properties being obtained from various modeling approaches using experimental and theoretical input. For example, methods based on machine learning (ML) use various sets of descriptors partly derived from ab initio calculations in order to fit experimental data. This approach, however, often requires large data sets and, most crucially, it is intrinsically interpolative and cannot give predictions outside the domain covered by an existing data set. A more transferable methodology is to use properties of elements, or simple compounds, for extrapolation of target properties to multi-component properties, mainly using the rule-of-mixture. Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. For example, ab initio and MD are very time-consuming and can hardly be used to predict structures of the alloys in a high-throughput manner. Phenomenological rules are based on empirical observations and are easy for calculations, but the accuracy of their predictions does not exceed 72% []. frame.system: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy, originally modeled as perfect crystals but now including real‐world defect features (e.g. 1 wt.% oxygen contamination) that are present in experimental specimens.
frame.goal: Develop a predictive method that accurately models the transport (conductivity) behavior of HfNbTaTiZr over two temperature regimes (near 0–200 K and 300–1200 K) by incorporating defect-induced scattering and microstructural disorder, thus overcoming the traditional reliance on perfect‐crystal analytical predictions.
frame.limitation: Existing analytical predictions are limited by assuming ideal, defect‐free crystals, leading to accuracy issues when compared with measurements on real specimens that have impurities (like oxygen) and inherent defects across wide temperature ranges.
root_cause_cues: limited accuracy of available analytical predictions
usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals
constraints: The method must be applicable in both the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime
It must explicitly account for non-idealities such as oxygen contamination and other defect types
The approach should predict temperature dependence and sample-specific effects, including defect scattering
Must offer predictions that can be benchmarked against measured conductivity data
frame.regime: Low-temperature regime (0–200 K) and high-temperature regime (300–1200 K)
prior_attempts: Analytical approaches based on perfect-crystal approximations that have failed to capture conductivity changes due to defects and oxygen contamination
Experimental measurements on oxygen-doped specimens that highlighted discrepancies when compared to predictions from idealized models
frame.understanding: The hypothesis is that a predictive approach which integrates first-principles data with defect and impurity scattering models (potentially using machine learning or uncertainty quantification methods) can more accurately model the conductivity behavior of HfNbTaTiZr across the specified temperature regimes. The approach should incorporate microscopic details such as defect concentrations and oxygen impurity levels, whose scattering contributions vary with temperature. Improvement over existing analytical methods would arise from its ability to quantitatively capture non-ideal lattice vibrational effects and defect-induced electron scattering, leading to predictions that are both temperature- and sample-specific.

additional_details.predicted_advantage: The new approach should outperform existing models by providing conductivity predictions that closely match measured values across both low and high temperature regimes, thereby reducing the systematic overestimation (or underestimation) stemming from ignoring defects.
additional_details.sample_applicability_limits: The hypothesis is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys with defect levels similar to or slightly exceeding 1 wt.% oxygen; outside this range, additional calibration may be required.
additional_details.temperature_limits: Predictions are expected to be reliable from near absolute zero (~0 K, practically starting around 0–200 K) up to 1200 K; deviations beyond these regimes would indicate limitations of the current scattering models.
additional_details.supporting_prior_evidence: Recent studies where machine-learning-enhanced ab initio methods successfully incorporated defect features to predict thermal and electronic transport in complex alloys; experimental benchmarks showing sensitivity of conductivity to oxygen content also support this approach.
additional_details.held_out_conductivity_benchmark: A falsification criterion would be if the approach predicts a room-temperature conductivity (e.g., at 300 K) within ±5% of experimental values for a defect-laden sample, but when applied to a held-out specimen with 1 wt.% oxygen, the measured conductivity deviates by more than 20% from the prediction. Such a discrepancy would falsify the hypothesis.
